meta.title: dix.tax: tax forms for owners who live abroad
meta.description: You own a flat or a house in a country you do not live in. Spain, Switzerland and Germany all want a return for it. dix.tax gives you the exact numbers, explained in your language. The Swiss declaration is ready today.

founder.title: Why I built this
body: I am Aleksej Dix. I live in Zurich and own flats in other countries. Every spring the same thing arrived: a form from a tax office in a country I do not live in, in a language that is not mine. I paid for the answers myself, in advisers and in evenings spent with directives.
Somebody who owns a flat in Zurich and lives abroad has exactly that problem, mirrored. The rules turn out to be simple once somebody explains them, and dix.tax puts what I learned into ten minutes.

footer.disclaimer: dix.tax is an information and calculation tool. It is not tax or legal advice and does not replace an adviser. Rules and practice can change; check your figures before you file.
footer.sources: Based on the Zurich tax return guide (Wegleitung) and the cantonal valuation directive.
footer.tagline: Tax forms for people who own property in a country they do not live in.

hub.title: You own property in a country you do not live in. That country still wants a tax return.
hub.lead: Spain, Switzerland and Germany all tax a property where it stands, whoever owns it and wherever they live. dix.tax prepares the Swiss declaration today: a few plain questions, the exact number for every line, explained in your language.
hub.ctaNote: About ten minutes. {price} per property. No account, and your figures stay in your browser.
hub.liveNote: Property in the canton of Zurich. Spain, Germany and the other cantons are in preparation.
hub.chooseLead: The Swiss declaration is ready today. Modelo 210 and Anlage V come next, and the answers below decide which one first.
hub.bothBody: A flat in Valencia owned from Berlin needs Modelo 210 in Spain, and it belongs in the German return as well. The two use different values and different rules. dix.tax keeps them apart and gets both right.

switzerland.name: Swiss tax return
switzerland.who: You own a flat or a house in the canton of Zurich and live in another country.
switzerland.what: The assessed values on the Liegenschaftenverzeichnis, the share of your debt Zurich accepts, and a German note for the tax office.

spain.name: Modelo 210
spain.who: You own a home in Spain and live somewhere else.
spain.what: Spain's tax for owners who are not resident there. Due every year, even if the home is never rented.

germany.name: Anlage V
germany.who: You rent out property in Germany and live somewhere else.
germany.what: The rental schedule of the German tax return, with depreciation and deductible costs.

deadlines.title: Deadlines coming up
deadlines.lead: The dates the tax administrations publish themselves. Extensions exist, but they have to be asked for in time.

labels.anlageVAdviser: German return {year}, filed by a tax adviser

deadlines.note: Your own deadline can differ if you asked for an extension or an adviser files for you.

trust.title: Why you can rely on the numbers

items.title: Every rule has a source
items.body: Each percentage and form line comes from an official guide, law or directive, and every calculator lists its sources.

items.title: Calculations are tested
items.body: Reference cases with known results run automatically on every change, so a fix in one place cannot quietly break another.

items.title: Your data stays with you
items.body: Your figures and addresses are calculated in your browser and never leave it. We only count anonymous events, such as which country a property is in.

items.title: A person stands behind it
items.body: dix.tax is built by Aleksej Dix in Zurich, who files these forms for his own properties.
